title: any English verb → + -en
hook: The single most productive rule in Dutch. A huge number of everyday English verbs are the same word with -en stuck on the end — because they're the same word, inherited from the same place. Say the English verb, add -en, and you have the Dutch infinitive.

examples.hint: Double the n so the first vowel stays short: begin-nen.
Same doubling: val-len.
The c is said as an s in English too — Dutch just spells it that way.

title: th → d
hook: Dutch has no "th" sound at all, and where English has one, Dutch nearly always has a plain d. This one rule unlocks a pile of the commonest words in the language.

examples.hint: Also the ou → ui shift: thou- → dui-.
The vowel opens up as well: i → e.

title: hard c → k
hook: Dutch spells the k sound with a k, always. Wherever English writes a hard c, write k — and the word is very often otherwise the same.

examples.hint: The vowel shifts too: English "old" → Dutch "oud". Also in old → oud.

title: ght → cht
hook: English kept a silent "gh" where it once had a throaty sound. Dutch still says it, and spells it "cht". Swap the letters and the word appears.

title: ou / ow → ui
hook: A sound shift that runs right through the language. "ui" is the hardest Dutch sound for an English mouth — start from the "ur" in "hurt" and round your lips hard.

examples.hint: Two rules at once: s → z as well.

title: oo → oe
hook: Dutch writes the "oo" sound as "oe". Careful: Dutch "oo" is a different sound entirely (as in "boot"), so the spelling swap matters.

examples.hint: The f softens to a v — that happens a lot at the start of a word.

title: long i → ij
hook: Where English says "eye", Dutch very often writes "ij" and says something between "ay" and "eye". It is a letter of its own — you'll see it capitalised as IJ.

examples.hint: Plus the -en from the verb rule.

title: long a → aa
hook: Dutch shows a long vowel by doubling it, rather than with a silent e on the end the way English does. Drop the English -e, double the a.

examples.hint: In an open syllable one a is already long: ma-ken. Doubled only when the syllable closes: "ik maak".
Here English has the ee and Dutch the aa — the same old vowel, gone two ways.

title: sh → sch
hook: Dutch has no "sh" sound. It writes "sch" and says both letters: an s, then the throaty ch of the g. Two sounds where English has one.

examples.hint: Plus oo → oe.
And the long vowel doubles: aa.
Same spelling, very different sound: "s-KHOHL".

title: s → z at the start
hook: English hardened an old z to an s at the front of words; Dutch kept the z. When an English word starts with an s sound and feels old and everyday, try z.

examples.hint: Also the "alt" → "out" shift you met in cold → koud.

title: ea / ee → ie
hook: Dutch writes the "ee" sound as "ie". And Dutch "ee" is a different sound again, closer to "ay" — so this swap is worth having in your fingers.

examples.hint: This one went to oe instead — the family is the same, the vowel wandered.
And Dutch still says the k: k-nee.

title: -ly → -lijk
hook: The same ending, worn down differently: English "-ly" and Dutch "-lijk" are both the old word for "body, form". Unstressed, so the ij goes lazy: say "-luk".

examples.hint: Dutch uses it where English says "of course" too.

title: -tion → -tie
hook: Every Latin word that came into English came into Dutch too. This ending is worth thousands of words — and you can guess them on the spot.

examples.hint: The odd one out: this one kept its English shape.

title: -ity → -iteit
hook: Another Latin ending, and another few hundred free words. The stress lands on the last syllable: kwali-TEIT.

examples.hint: Dutch writes the kw sound as kw, never qu.

title: -ize / -ise → -eren
rule: English "-ize", "-ise", and many Latin verbs  →  Dutch "-eren"
hook: If a verb feels Latin or international, this is almost always the way in. The stress goes on the -EER-.

title: -ic / -ical → -isch
hook: Don't be fooled by the spelling — "-isch" is said "-ees", with no ch sound at all. Once you accept that, a whole shelf of adjectives is yours.

title: -y → -ig
hook: The ending that turns a noun into an adjective. Unstressed, so it goes lazy: "-ukh".

examples.hint: You'll more often just say "Ik heb honger" — I have hunger.
Double the n to keep the o short.

title: a little one → -je
rule: any noun + "-je"  →  a small, nice, or casual one of them
hook: The most Dutch habit there is. Stick -je on the end and the thing becomes small, or friendly, or just an ordinary portion of it — a biertje is simply the beer you order.

title: w is said "v", v is said "f"
rule: written "w"  →  say a soft "v"   ·   written "v"  →  say "f"
hook: Nothing changes in the spelling here — this is purely what comes out of your mouth. Get these two right and you immediately sound less English.

examples.hint: Say "VAH-ter".
Say "vat".
Say "FAH-der" — the v is an f.
Say "feyf". Both rules in one word.

title: g is throaty
rule: written "g" or "ch"  →  a scraped, throaty sound
hook: The sound Dutch is famous for. It's the ch in Scottish "loch" or German "Bach", made at the back of the throat — and in the north it's scraped hard enough to sound like clearing your throat. There is no soft English g in Dutch at all.

examples.hint: Say "khoot" — throaty g, and the d at the end goes to t.
Say "khrahkh" — one at each end.
Say "KHAY-vuh".

title: final d → t, final b → p
rule: a "d" or "b" at the end of a word  →  say "t" or "p"
hook: Dutch keeps the letter but hardens the sound at the end of a word. Spelling stays put — this is only about what you say — and it explains why hond and hont sound identical.

examples.hint: Say "hont".
Say "hant".
Say "ik hep".
Say "khoot". Add the g rule and you have the whole word.
